extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method; philosophers of science; experimental investigators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the four classical inductive methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues) and their joint use to establish causal laws, with examples and conditions for correct experimental design and inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction from ascertained properties of agents present
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduce the effect from the ascertained properties of the agents known to be present; this form of deductive proof shows causation as well as co-existence and can account for exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Theory of Dew — deducing that cooling of a surface (given the hygrometric condition of the air) will cause aqueous vapor to condense. Advantage: at once proves causation and co-existence and accounts for exceptions (e.g., very dry air yields no dew). Use alongside experiment and observation to strengthen inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference (direct experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare two cases which differ only in the presence of the suspected antecedent (A B C vs B C), so that the difference in outcome can be attributed to that antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct experiment corroborates causation (e.g., cooling a surface until dew forms). Requirements and examples: the two limbs of the same animal were presumed to differ in no circumstance material to the case except the paralysis; repeat experiments sufficiently often in different subjects to exclude accidental differences. Natural phenomena can sometimes provide such an experiment (e.g., clouds withdrawing cause surface cooling and dew) if they introduce a single definite new circumstance rapidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple instances exhibiting the same effect all share a single common circumstance, infer that the common circumstance is connected with the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to identify a common antecedent (e.g., exhausted animals that rapidly putrefy after killing all share preceding exhaustive exertion). Limitation: by itself it is not competent to prove causation — it only identifies candidate antecedents. It is stronger when causation is already known by other means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer causal connection when variations in one phenomenon are accompanied by corresponding variations in another (the degree of antecedent variation correlates with the degree of consequent variation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: galvanic charge strength correlated with shortening of cadaveric rigidity and acceleration of putrefaction; the principle is used to infer proportional dependency. Use graded/intensity-controlled experiments to observe concomitant changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine Agreement and Difference: show that cases which agree in the effect agree only in a suspected antecedent, and that when that antecedent is absent (or reversed) the effect does not follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: muscular irritability at death — cases with late and long rigidity agree only in high irritability; cases with early brief rigidity agree only in low irritability. The joint method provides stronger inductive support (and in contexts where the aggregate antecedent is already known to cause the effect, it helps isolate which part of the antecedent is responsible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtract from an observed effect the portions already accounted for by known causes; the remaining 'residual' phenomenon suggests the existence of additional causes to be investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: anomalies in cometary return suggesting resistance of a medium; Arago's magnetic needle experiments showing retarding influence of copper; Laplace explaining residual sound-velocity via heat developed in compression; discovery of chemical elements in residues. Requires estimating/calculating effects of known causes (ideally a priori) and examining what remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of natural experiments when they satisfy Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: When nature introduces a single, perfectly definite new circumstance and manifests its effect rapidly, that natural occurrence can serve as a test equivalent to an experimental Method of Difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the temporary withdrawal of clouds creating a clear opening and immediate deposition of dew. Criterion: the natural change must be singular and rapid enough to preclude other material changes in antecedent circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure complete resemblance except the one antecedent (avoid single-pair overconfidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Method of Difference designs, do not assume that two instances differ in no material respect except the suspected antecedent from a single pair; secure this assumption by careful control and repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brown-Séquard: comparing paralysed and opposite healthy limb presumes no material differences other than paralysis; to exclude accidental pathological differences repeat experiments across many animals. Anti-pattern: drawing conclusion from a single unreplicated comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal and counter-evidence as strong confirmation (A B C vs a b c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that when the antecedent is reversed or an opposite antecedent supplied, a contrary consequent follows, strengthening causal attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after paralysis initially increased irritability then months later decreased irritability and reversed effects on rigidity — gives A B C, a b c and B C, b c of the Method of Difference. Demonstrating reversal helps rule out confounding causes that always accompany the antecedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by multiple independent lines (deduction, direct experiment, natural observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine deductive reasoning from agent-properties, small-scale controlled experiments, and large-scale/natural observations to build accumulated proof of a causal theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dew theory: deduction from properties of agents present, direct laboratory cooling experiments, and natural atmospheric observations together provide a high degree of assurance. Use diverse methods to account for exceptions and increase confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate and allow for known causes before assigning residuals
rubrics_metrics.description: For the Method of Residues to be valid, estimate the effects of known causes (ideally a priori from laws established separately), subtract them from observation, and examine the remaining residual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arago example: to make it an instance of Residues rather than Difference, the effects of air resistance and thread rigidity should be calculated a priori and subtracted to reveal the copper's influence. Residual analysis depends on reliable quantification of known contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological humility: induction needs tests akin to syllogistic tests for deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive inferences should be judged by explicit rules and models (like the Four Methods) so that inductive arguments can be rendered conclusive when they conform to those criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill's defense against Whewell: the Four Methods serve as tests of inductive evidence similar to syllogistic tests for deduction. Do not accept inductions without subjecting them to these methods; erroneous inductions are common without such tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the Methods — Agreement alone cannot prove causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the Method of Agreement (and the Joint Method insofar as it is an improvement of Agreement) cannot, by itself, establish causation unless supplemented by other methods showing causal linkage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Agreement to identify candidate antecedents, but seek Difference, Concomitant Variations, or known causal background to convert that identification into a causal proof. Mill stresses contexts where causation is already known (e.g., death causes cadaveric changes), Agreement then helps isolate the particular causal factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use graded/quantitative experimental variation to infer proportional relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ experiments with varied intensities of an antecedent to observe proportional changes in the consequent and infer a quantitative relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brown-Séquard's galvanic experiments: more powerful charges produced shorter rigidity and faster putrefaction; such concomitant variation supports proportional causal claims. Design experiments to vary the antecedent across a range and record consequent magnitudes.
